issues.legal_issue: Official ownership records and the surrounding documentary evidence established that the suit property belonged to the religious endowment.
material_facts: Public village and inam records consistently identified the deity as the registered inamdar of the land.
The inam title deed and pattas were issued to the deity, and records described the land as religious endowment property.
The defendants' documents contained unilateral recitals about the family's interest and acknowledged that the village accounts recorded the deity as inamdar.
issues.conclusion: The deity was the owner of the suit lands.
issues.legal_principle: Consistent official ownership records, supported by title documents and admissions in the opposing party's documents, were not displaced by unilateral declarations that had not been shown to have been brought to the endowment's authorities. The Court relied on the documentary evidence in the record.

predicates.ownership_dispute: The parties disputed who owned property held or claimed by a religious endowment.
predicates.official_records_name_endowment_as_owner: Public records identify the religious endowment as the property's owner or registered holder.
predicates.title_documents_support_endowment_owners: Title documents or official grants support the religious endowment's ownership.
predicates.opposing_claim_rests_on_unilateral_decla: The opposing party relies on unilateral statements that do not displace the official ownership evidence.

issues.definition: When an ownership dispute concerns property for which official records and title documents identify the religious endowment as owner, unilateral opposing declarations do not prevent the endowment from being found to own the property.

issues.legal_issue: A written grant whose terms are withheld by the claimant did not establish a permanent tenancy and instead created a year-to-year lease.
material_facts: The defendants claimed that an 1851 sanad gave their predecessor a permanent interest in the lands.
The defendants' family had possessed the lands for generations and supplied oil to the temple in return.
The public records continued to identify the deity as inamdar, and the pattas were issued to the deity.
Despite notice and evidence that the sanad had been in the defendants' family's possession, the defendants did not produce it.
The proved arrangement was consistent with a lease, and the temple manager had authority in ordinary management to grant a year-to-year agricultural lease.
issues.conclusion: The sanad granted a year-to-year lease in return for the daily supply of oil, not a permanent tenancy or a conveyance of ownership.
issues.legal_principle: Where a tenancy originates in a written instrument, its duration is determined by construing that instrument; the parties' circumstances and subsequent conduct may assist if its language is ambiguous. Long possession and related circumstances may support an inference of permanent tenancy when the origin is unknown, but here the instrument was known and deliberately withheld, warranting presumptions against the party withholding it. A manager may grant an ordinary year-to-year lease in the course of managing an endowment, but a permanent lease ordinarily requires legal necessity. The Court referred to Sivayogeswara Cotton Press v. M. Panchaksharappa; Bjoy Gopal Mukherji v. Pratul Chandra Ghose; Maharanee Shibissouree Debia v. Mothooranath Acharjoo; Naini Pillai Marakayar v. Ramanathan Chettiar; Bawa Sitaram v. Kasturbhai Manibhai; and Muhammad Muzaffar-Al-Musavi v. Jabeda Khatun.

rule.if: claim_under_written_grant and religious_property_recorded_to_endowment and grant_document_withheld_by_claimant and proved_arrangement_consistent_with_ordinary_lease

predicates.claim_under_written_grant: A party claims that a written grant created an interest in property.
predicates.religious_property_recorded_to_endowment: Official records identify the property as belonging to a religious endowment.
predicates.grant_document_withheld_by_claimant: The party relying on the grant withholds the document despite having it or being shown to possess it.
predicates.proved_arrangement_consistent_with_ordin: The established arrangement is consistent with an ordinary lease rather than a permanent transfer.

issues.definition: If a claimant relies on a withheld written grant concerning property recorded to a religious endowment and the proved arrangement is consistent with an ordinary lease, the grant creates a year-to-year tenancy.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant in continuing possession could not acquire the landlord endowment's title by asserting a hostile claim without openly surrendering possession or maintaining an openly adverse basis for possession.
material_facts: The defendants and their predecessors possessed the lands under a year-to-year tenancy from the temple.
A tenant asserted in a notice to the religious endowments authority that the land had been granted to his predecessor, but the temple trustees were not served with that notice.
The authority later adopted a scheme identifying the lands as the deity's property, and the tenant raised no objection to that scheme.
The evidence did not establish that the tenant thereafter possessed the lands on a notorious claim of absolute title or permanent tenancy.
The tenancy continued until it was terminated by notice.
issues.conclusion: The defendants did not acquire title by adverse possession during the tenancy, and their assertion of a hostile claim did not convert the tenancy into a permanent one.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a tenant in possession cannot deny the landlord's title at the beginning of the tenancy while the tenancy continues. A tenant cannot obtain a permanent right of occupancy in derogation of the landlord's title merely by asserting such a right to the landlord's knowledge. The Court relied on Bilas Kunwar v. Desraj Ranjit Singh; Mohammad Mumtaz Ali Khan v. Mohan Singh; Madhavrao Waman Satindalgekar v. Raghunath Venkatesh Deshpande; Naini Pillai Marakayar v. Ramanathan Chettiar; and Patna Municipal Corporation v. Ram Das.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_possession_dispute and possession_under_continuing_tenancy and tenant_asserts_hostile_title_without_surrender and hostile_possession_not_openly_maintained

predicates.landlord_tenant_possession_dispute: The proceeding concerns a landlord seeking possession from a tenant.
predicates.possession_under_continuing_tenancy: The occupant remains in possession under a tenancy that has not ended.
predicates.tenant_asserts_hostile_title_without_sur: The tenant asserts ownership or a permanent right against the landlord without openly surrendering possession.
predicates.hostile_possession_not_openly_maintained: The evidence does not show that the tenant openly and notoriously maintained possession on a hostile basis.

issues.definition: A tenant who remains in possession under a continuing tenancy does not acquire the landlord's title by adverse possession merely by asserting a hostile claim without surrendering possession or openly maintaining hostile possession.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord's suit to recover property after a lawful lease by a prior manager was governed by the limitation rule for recovery from a tenant, not the rule for recovery after an unauthorised transfer by a manager.
material_facts: The temple manager had authority to grant the year-to-year lease in the ordinary course of management, and the lease bound the temple.
The lease continued after the manager left office and remained effective until terminated by notice.
The suit was brought by the landlord to recover possession from the tenant after termination of the tenancy.
The suit was instituted within the time allowed for a landlord's recovery action against a tenant.
issues.conclusion: The rule concerning recovery after an unauthorised transfer by a previous manager did not apply; the landlord's suit was governed by the limitation rule for recovery from a tenant and was timely.
issues.legal_principle: Article 134-B of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, concerns an illegal or unauthorised transfer by a previous manager and does not apply where a lawful transfer remains effective after the manager leaves office. A suit by a landlord to recover possession from a tenant is governed by Article 139; the Court held that the suit was timely because it followed termination of the tenancy and was filed within the applicable period. The Court also considered section 28 and Article 144 in addressing the claim that title had been extinguished by adverse possession.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_recovery_suit and prior_manager_made_lawful_lease and lease_remained_effective_after_manager_left and tenancy_terminated_before_suit and suit_filed_within_applicable_recovery_period

predicates.landlord_tenant_recovery_suit: The proceeding is a landlord's suit to recover possession from a tenant.
predicates.prior_manager_made_lawful_lease: A previous manager made a lease that was within the manager's authority and bound the property owner.
predicates.lease_remained_effective_after_manager_l: The lease remained in force after the manager left office.
predicates.tenancy_terminated_before_suit: The tenancy ended before the landlord filed the recovery suit.
predicates.suit_filed_within_applicable_recovery_pe: The landlord filed the suit within the time allowed for recovery after the tenancy ended.

issues.definition: When a landlord sues to recover possession from a tenant under a lawful lease that remained effective after the manager left office, the applicable landlord-tenant limitation rule governs, and a suit filed within its allowed period is timely.
